title: Bangkok Declares Flood Disaster After 12 Inches of Rain
summary:
Bangkok is built on a network of canals — and right now, those canals are full.

A flood emergency disaster has been declared across the Thai capital after more than 300 millimeters (12 inches) of rain fell since Thursday, leaving roads submerged. Canals across the city have burst their banks, leaving roads under water. On Sunday, Bangkok's Metropolitan Authority said the rains had subsided, but canal water levels remain high. The city's governor warned the flooding is not over.

People have been urged to stay home, and those living close to canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors. All 50 of Bangkok's districts were declared emergency zones. On Saturday, Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said the east of the city was hardest hit. "The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best," he said. "We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full... The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled."

Somkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, told the AFP news agency: "The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now. I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now." She said the water appeared worse than in 2011, when nationwide flooding killed hundreds across Thailand over three months.

So far, no casualties have been reported in Bangkok from this latest flooding. Thunderstorms are common in Thailand at this time of year, but extreme weather in recent days has overwhelmed Bangkok's drainage system, causing traffic chaos on roads that are already famously congested. The Thai Meteorological Service has forecast more heavy rain through the week, though the low-pressure area causing the downpours is expected to move toward central Thailand.
why_it_matters: Bangkok is a megacity and a national economic hub, so when its drainage system is overwhelmed, transport, shops and daily work stop for millions of people — and the article's comparison with 2011 shows how quickly a few days of rain can echo an entire season of disaster. The combination of sinking ground, rising seas and heavier downpours is a problem many coastal cities will face, so how Bangkok adapts is being watched as a test case.

background_read: Bangkok (Thailand's capital and its largest city) grew up around a dense web of canals, called 'khlong' in Thai, which once carried boats and trade the way roads carry cars today. That canal network is also part of the city's drainage system — which is why every canal filling up quickly becomes a flooding problem on the streets.

Bangkok sits on soft clay in the delta of the Chao Phraya River, and the ground under parts of the city is slowly sinking while sea levels rise, so storm water has fewer places to go. The Bangkok Metropolitan Authority (the city's local government) runs the pumps and emergency response, under Governor Chadchart Sittipunt, the city's elected leader, who warned that the flooding is not over.

Thailand's rainy season regularly brings thunderstorms, but extreme downpours can overwhelm the drains, and roads in Bangkok are already famously congested even in dry weather. The 2011 floods mentioned in the article were nationwide and lasted months, killing hundreds of people, so residents who lived through them are a sharp measuring stick for how serious a flood is.

The Thai Meteorological Service (the government agency that issues Thailand's weather forecasts) is watching a low-pressure area; AFP (Agence France-Presse, a global news agency) interviewed residents for the story.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — the emergency response is working
perspectives.description: Authorities declared emergency zones in all 50 districts, told people near canals to move belongings upstairs and urged everyone to stay home, and so far no casualties have been reported in Bangkok. The governor has been visible and direct about the limits of the response — admitting the canals are full while crews keep pumping — which at least gives residents clear information.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — the city was not ready
perspectives.description: Extreme rain overwhelmed Bangkok's drainage system, submerging roads in a city that is already famous for traffic jams, and residents near canals — often the least able to move — were the hardest hit. One 67-year-old shop owner described waist-deep water and two days of lost business, and said this looked worse than the 2011 floods that killed hundreds, raising questions about what has been fixed since.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — a structural problem, not a freak event
perspectives.description: Bangkok was built around canals on soft clay, the ground beneath parts of the city is sinking and sea levels are rising, so heavy monsoon rain becomes far more dangerous than it would be elsewhere. Thunderstorms are normal at this time of year, which means the real variable is how much water the drainage system can absorb — a question of planning, land use and maintenance as much as weather.

More heavy rain is forecast through the week, and the low-pressure area causing it is expected to move toward central Thailand, so the immediate job is pumping and protecting canal-side neighbourhoods. Longer term, cities like Bangkok face choices about bigger drains, water storage, restoring canal space and limiting construction on flood paths — expensive decisions that will be judged the next time a storm like this arrives.
